candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the catalog/schemaPattern/tableNamePattern strings only where the application forwards untrusted input to DatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges (typical for DB explorer/admin UIs, metadata-driven portals, or multi-tenant code that passes a user-supplied table/schema name). Those strings are then treated as SQL text by the driver. No Snowflake-side attacker control is required.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that (a) sibling metadata methods use escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand while getTablePrivileges does not; (b) unescapeChars/escapeSqlQuotes escape only double quotes, not single quotes; (c) tableNamePattern is used raw with no earlier Wildcard/identifier sanitization; (d) the post-filter at lines 2032-2047 compares table_name/schema to the raw attacker string, which limits UNION-style exfiltration; (e) executeAndReturnEmptyResultIfNotFound swallows only NO_DATA/BASE_TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND-style exceptions, so other injection-induced errors do propagate to the caller; (f) this is a single-statement SELECT under default settings, so impact is bounded and no runtime confirmation was performed.
candidates.impact: SQL injection in the context of the application's Snowflake session using the driver: manipulation of the metadata query, blind/error-based inference of data the session can read, forced expensive queries or errors (denial of service). Direct bulk extraction through the returned ResultSet is constrained because next() post-filters rows on the raw pattern values (lines 2032-2047), and stacked-statement execution depends on the session's multi-statement setting; this is an injection lead, not a demonstrated account takeover.
candidates.prerequisites: Application code calls java.sql.DatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges with attacker-influenced tableNamePattern or schemaPattern (both non-null, not empty, not exactly "%" or ".*"). A normal authenticated session must exist; this is not an authentication bypass. Result visibility or exception/timing differences are needed for blind exploitation.
candidates.root_cause: getTablePrivileges builds the query string by concatenating caller-supplied patterns directly into single-quoted SQL string literals. Line 1989 inserts tableNamePattern raw ("where table_name = '" + tableNamePattern + "'"), and lines 1997/1999 insert schemaPattern after unescapeChars(). unescapeChars (lines 238-244) only reverses \_, \% and \\ escapes and doubles double quotes via escapeSqlQuotes (lines 248-250); it does not escape single quotes, so a quote in either parameter terminates the literal. The class already has an explicit anti-injection helper, escapeSingleQuoteForLikeCommand (lines 258-274, javadoc: "This guards against SQL injections by ensuring that any single quote is escaped properly"), which is used for the same kind of user input in getProcedures/getTables/getColumns/getStreams/getSchemas (lines 1425, 1538, 1716, 2893, 3297) but is omitted here. The resulting string is executed by executeAndReturnEmptyResultIfNotFound -> statement.executeQuery(sql) (lines 3657-3665) called from line 2009.
candidates.title: SQL injection in DatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges via unescaped table/schema pattern
candidates.trace: Caller string (e.g. a table name containing ') -> line 1989 concatenation into "select * from <catalog>.information_schema.table_privileges where table_name = '<input>'" (and/or lines 1997/1999 for table_schema) -> line 2009 executeAndReturnEmptyResultIfNotFound -> line 3665 statement.executeQuery(sql) -> SQL is parsed/executed server-side in the application's Snowflake session. A crafted quote breaks out of the literal and lets the WHERE clause be modified with additional boolean predicates/subqueries, which can be observed through returned rows, propagated SQLExceptions, or timing (blind/error-based inference). No weaponized payload is included here.
candidates.unverified: Static review only: no code execution or server interaction, so the exact Snowflake parser behavior for crafted patterns, the effect of multi-statement settings, and the real-world exploitability magnitude are unverified. Whether upstream considers this a vulnerability or intended caller responsibility is unknown, and no application passing untrusted values was inspected. Line numbers refer to this snapshot only.

coverage_summary: All 345 model-visible files in the assigned tree were enumerated; coverage focused on main Java sources (src/main/java), with resources and build/CI files skimmed for context. Repo-wide literal searches were run for command execution, reflection/deserialization (ObjectInputStream/readObject), XML parsing, URL/HTTP sinks, file writes/temp files, credential storage, TLS/OCSP handling, and SQL construction, then the strongest regions were read in detail: SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData (full SQL-building sections and all DatabaseMetaData methods), SnowflakeConnectionV1, SFAsyncResultSet/QueryIdValidator, SessionUtil and SessionUtilExternalBrowser, SFTrustManager OCSP flow, FileCacheManager/CredentialManager/secure storage, SnowflakeFileTransferAgent plus S3/Azure/GCS clients, RestRequest/HttpUtil, DefaultResultStreamProvider, IncidentUtil/EventHandler, config parsers, and telemetry. No test sources are present in the snapshot.
limitations: Static, read-only review: no compilation, execution, tests, scanners or live Snowflake server interaction, so all findings are unconfirmed leads.
No test directory, git history, diff, release notes or patch data is present, so the intended fix/vulnerability cannot be confirmed; line numbers apply only to this snapshot.

Large files (SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData 137 KB, SnowflakeFileTransferAgent 130 KB, SessionUtil 77 KB, SFTrustManager 67 KB, SFSession 56 KB) were reviewed in security-relevant regions rather than line-by-line end to end.
Exploitability magnitude depends on server-side SQL grammar, multi-statement settings and application call patterns that cannot be exercised here.
Binary-like files are skipped by the tooling; no source files were reported as excluded by the scope filters (0 over 5 MiB, 0 sensitive-name, 0 symlink exclusions).

rejected_leads.lead: SnowflakeConnectionV1.setCatalog (line 441) and setSchema (lines 758-760) concatenate caller strings inside double-quoted identifiers without escaping embedded double quotes, in contrast to SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData which uses escapeSqlQuotes for identifier contexts.
rejected_leads.reason: Same CWE-89 class and user-input dependent, but the sink is a USE DATABASE/USE SCHEMA statement where quote breakout mostly yields grammar errors unless multi-statement execution is enabled; no explicit missed-sanitization helper exists in that class. Not selected because the getTablePrivileges omission has stronger in-file evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: DiagnosticTrustManager accepts all certificates and CertificateDiagnosticCheck installs it as the JVM-wide HttpsURLConnection default SSLSocketFactory during a diagnostic run (lines 34-56).
rejected_leads.reason: Real CWE-295 concern (global, racy, restored in finally), but it is confined to the optional diagnostic tool whose purpose is to fetch/print untrusted certs; not reachable from normal JDBC connection paths in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultAuthExternalBrowserHandlers.openBrowser builds OS commands by concatenating the server-provided ssoUrl (lines 71-94).
rejected_leads.reason: URLUtil.isValidURL restricts the string to a URL charset that excludes spaces, semicolons, pipes and backticks, Runtime.exec(String) does not invoke a shell, and the URL originates from the Snowflake service response; no shell-metacharacter injection traced.

rejected_leads.lead: SessionUtil.federatedFlowStep3 concatenates username/password into a JSON string for the IdP token request (lines 1286-1293).
rejected_leads.reason: JSON/request injection affects only the caller's own credentials in an outbound IdP call; no cross-privilege impact established.

rejected_leads.lead: OCSP fail-open is the default (SFBaseSession.getOCSPMode lines 739-748).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented product behavior/config decision, with FAIL_CLOSED available; not a code-level validation defect.

rejected_leads.lead: File-transfer path handling (SnowflakeFileTransferAgent destFileName derived via lastIndexOf("/") and concatenated to user/localLocation; storage clients write localLocation + "\" + destFileName).
rejected_leads.reason: The direction and location are user-specified for GET/PUT, and verifyLocalFilePath guards server tampering; no concrete cross-boundary traversal was traced in the inspected paths.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL built in getSecondResultSetCommand from catalog/schema/procedure values (lines 1450-1467) and SFAsyncResultSet result_scan (line 192).
rejected_leads.reason: Values come from server-returned metadata in the first case, and the public String query-ID constructor is gated by QueryIdValidator (lines 81-89); no attacker-controlled path found.

summary: Reviewed the snowflake-jdbc 3.21.1-SNAPSHOT source tree (345 model-visible files: main Java under src/main/java, resources, build/CI config). One candidate is submitted: SQL injection via unescaped string-literal concatenation in SnowflakeDatabaseMetaData.getTablePrivileges. Other suspicious areas (setCatalog/setSchema identifier concatenation, diagnostic trust manager, external-browser command URL, SSO JSON building, OCSP fail-open, file-transfer path handling) were inspected and are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads rather than additional candidates.
